name: code-review-design-graph
description: A bounded discovery graph from observable review pressures to SOLID principle hypotheses and candidate design patterns. Matches require confirmation against the code and are never findings by themselves.

nodes.name: Varying behavior
nodes.summary: Multiple interchangeable behaviors are selected by branching or duplicated orchestration.
cues: switch or if chains choose an algorithm or policy
the same operation has multiple replaceable implementations
new variants repeatedly modify a central dispatcher

nodes.name: State-dependent behavior
nodes.summary: An object's valid behavior changes with explicit state and transition rules.
cues: methods repeat branches on a state or status field
state transitions and allowed operations are scattered
adding a state requires editing many unrelated methods

nodes.name: Creation policy variation
nodes.summary: Callers choose concrete types or related object families using repeated construction policy.
cues: callers switch on type before construction
concrete constructors leak into application policy
related products must remain compatible as a family

nodes.name: Complex construction
nodes.summary: A valid object requires ordered assembly, many optional parts, or cross-field validation.
cues: constructors have many optional or mutually constrained parameters
callers repeat multi-step assembly in different places
partially initialized objects can escape

nodes.name: Incompatible boundary
nodes.summary: An external or legacy interface does not match the contract expected by local code.
cues: vendor API details leak across many callers
translation between external and internal models is duplicated
tests must mock a broad third party surface

nodes.name: Optional responsibilities
nodes.summary: Independent optional behaviors must be combined without multiplying subclasses or branches.
cues: subclasses represent every combination of independent features
wrapping behavior is repeated around the same operation
features must be enabled per instance at runtime

nodes.name: Subsystem coupling
nodes.summary: Clients coordinate many internal subsystem types to perform a common operation.
cues: many callers repeat the same subsystem call sequence
clients depend on internal subsystem structure
a simple use case requires many collaborators

nodes.name: Recursive part-whole structure
nodes.summary: Leaves and containers form a tree and should support the same meaningful operations.
cues: client code branches between leaf and collection types
nested objects recursively aggregate child results
tree operations are duplicated across node kinds

nodes.name: Event fanout
nodes.summary: One producer must notify a changing set of consumers without owning their concrete behavior.
cues: a producer directly calls several unrelated consumers
consumers are added or removed independently
notification wiring is duplicated or tightly coupled

nodes.name: Request lifecycle
nodes.summary: Operations need identity so they can be queued, retried, logged, scheduled, or undone.
cues: callbacks carry growing request metadata
retry or audit logic duplicates operation dispatch
requests must be stored or composed before execution

nodes.name: Ordered processing chain
nodes.summary: A request passes through ordered handlers until one handles it or each contributes processing.
cues: a dispatcher contains an expanding ordered if chain
handlers must be reordered or composed independently
middleware repeats forwarding and stop conditions

nodes.name: Dependency construction coupling
nodes.summary: Business behavior constructs concrete collaborators whose lifecycle and implementation belong elsewhere.
cues: methods instantiate network filesystem clock or database clients
tests require global patching to replace collaborators
dependency lifecycle is mixed with domain behavior

nodes.name: Persistence coupling
nodes.summary: Use-case or domain code depends directly on storage queries, records, or ORM mechanics.
cues: queries and mapping repeat across application services
domain decisions depend on ORM or database types
persistence changes force unrelated business changes

nodes.name: Single Responsibility Principle
nodes.summary: A unit should have one cohesive responsibility and one reason to change.
cues: one unit combines responsibilities that change for distinct stakeholders or policies
a change to one responsibility repeatedly forces edits or regression risk in another
unrelated behavior must be coordinated because it is owned by the same unit
guardrails: require distinct responsibilities or reasons to change and demonstrate their concrete maintenance or correctness cost
do not infer a violation from file size method count or number of collaborators alone

nodes.name: Open/Closed Principle
aliases: open for extension closed for modification
nodes.summary: Stable policy should support demonstrated extensions without repeated invasive modification.
cues: new variants repeatedly require edits to a central branch or stable policy
the same extension repeatedly modifies several established components
extension friction is visible in the current diff or repository history
guardrails: require demonstrated recurring extension friction and its concrete maintenance or correctness cost
do not introduce extension points for hypothetical reuse or variants

nodes.name: Liskov Substitution Principle
nodes.summary: A subtype must preserve the contracts and compatible behavior expected through its base type.
cues: a subtype strengthens preconditions weakens postconditions or breaks a base invariant
a subtype rejects an operation that the base contract promises
base-typed callers require subtype checks or special handling to remain correct
guardrails: identify the violated base contract invariant or incompatible behavior and demonstrate the resulting cost
different implementation details performance or internal state alone are not violations

nodes.name: Interface Segregation Principle
nodes.summary: Consumers should depend only on the operations relevant to their actual needs.
cues: a consumer must depend on members it does not use or cannot meaningfully support
an implementation throws or supplies dummy behavior for inapplicable interface members
interface changes repeatedly affect consumers unrelated to the changed capability
guardrails: identify an actual consumer burden and demonstrate its maintenance or correctness cost
a broad interface alone is insufficient without unused inapplicable or change-coupled members

nodes.name: Dependency Inversion Principle
nodes.summary: High-level policy should not depend directly on replaceable low-level implementation details.
cues: business policy imports or constructs replaceable database network filesystem or framework details
changing a low-level implementation forces unrelated high-level policy changes
testing or substitution requires patching concrete infrastructure inside policy code
guardrails: identify high-level policy coupled to a replaceable low-level detail and demonstrate the resulting cost
do not equate dependency inversion with dependency injection because injection alone does not establish dependency direction

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.summary: Encapsulate interchangeable behavior behind one contract and let the caller select the policy.
applicability: behavior varies independently from the context that uses it
new variants otherwise require editing a central conditional
tradeoffs: adds contracts and objects that callers must understand
selection and lifecycle policy still need a clear owner
avoid_when: the branch is stable, local, and unlikely to gain variants
variants do not share a meaningful behavioral contract

nodes.name: State
nodes.summary: Move state-specific behavior and transitions into objects representing valid states.
applicability: the same operations behave differently across explicit states
transition rules or state branches are scattered across methods
tradeoffs: creates more types and makes transition ownership a design decision
cross-state invariants can become harder to see
avoid_when: there are only simple data states with no distinct behavior
a compact transition table expresses the rules more clearly

nodes.name: Factory Method
nodes.summary: Centralize selection and creation of one product behind a stable creation operation.
applicability: concrete construction varies while the consuming workflow remains stable
callers should depend on a product contract instead of constructors
tradeoffs: moves rather than removes creation policy
subclass-based forms can introduce unnecessary inheritance
avoid_when: direct construction is already simple and stable
the factory would only rename a constructor without owning policy

nodes.name: Abstract Factory
nodes.summary: Create compatible families of related products through one family-level contract.
applicability: multiple related products must vary together as a compatible family
clients must remain independent of family-specific concrete types
tradeoffs: adding a new product kind changes every factory family
introduces several contracts and coordinated implementations
avoid_when: only one independently varying product is created
family compatibility is not a real invariant

nodes.name: Builder
nodes.summary: Separate staged construction from the final representation and enforce valid assembly at completion.
applicability: construction has many optional or ordered steps
several representations share an assembly process
tradeoffs: adds a construction API and often duplicates field names
validation timing must remain explicit
avoid_when: a small constructor or named factory is clearer
the builder permits invalid combinations instead of preventing them

nodes.name: Adapter
nodes.summary: Translate an external or legacy interface into the focused contract expected by local code.
applicability: a useful dependency exposes an incompatible interface or model
translation should be localized at a system boundary
tradeoffs: adds mapping code and another failure boundary
can hide important external semantics if the local contract is too narrow
avoid_when: the local interface merely duplicates the external API
callers genuinely require the full external contract

nodes.name: Decorator
nodes.summary: Compose optional responsibilities by wrapping the same behavioral contract.
applicability: orthogonal behaviors must be combined per instance
subclass combinations are multiplying
tradeoffs: execution order becomes significant and may be difficult to inspect
many small wrappers complicate debugging and identity
avoid_when: features are not independent or composable
one explicit orchestration function is easier to follow

nodes.name: Facade
nodes.summary: Expose a focused entry point for common subsystem workflows while keeping lower-level APIs available when needed.
applicability: many clients repeat the same subsystem orchestration
internal subsystem structure leaks into ordinary use cases
tradeoffs: can become a broad god service if unrelated workflows accumulate
may obscure capabilities or errors that callers need
avoid_when: clients use genuinely different low-level capabilities
the proposed facade has no cohesive use-case boundary

nodes.name: Composite
nodes.summary: Represent leaves and containers through one meaningful contract so clients can operate on a tree uniformly.
applicability: the domain is naturally recursive and part-whole
leaf and container operations share valid semantics
tradeoffs: a common contract may admit operations that do not fit every node
parent ownership and cycle prevention require care
avoid_when: leaf and container behavior is fundamentally different
uniformity would weaken type safety or domain invariants

nodes.name: Observer
nodes.summary: Notify a changing set of subscribers through an event contract without coupling the producer to concrete consumers.
applicability: one event has multiple independently evolving consumers
subscriber registration or replacement must be dynamic
tradeoffs: ordering, failure handling, and delivery semantics become implicit unless defined
subscriber lifecycle can cause leaks or hidden work
avoid_when: the producer requires one explicit mandatory collaborator
transactional ordering or failure propagation must remain direct

nodes.name: Command
nodes.summary: Represent a request as an object so execution can be queued, retried, logged, composed, or undone.
applicability: operations need identity and lifecycle beyond an immediate call
dispatch must be separated from execution
tradeoffs: adds request types and serialization or versioning concerns
undo requires explicit compensating state rather than automatic reversal
avoid_when: a direct method call already expresses the full lifecycle
commands would be data-free wrappers with no operational need

nodes.name: Chain of Responsibility
nodes.summary: Compose ordered handlers that process or forward a request without a central branch over concrete handlers.
applicability: the handler set or order changes independently
the first capable handler or an ordered pipeline processes a request
tradeoffs: handler order and termination can become hidden behavior
a request may be silently unhandled without an explicit terminal policy
avoid_when: dispatch rules are small, fixed, and clearer as direct branching
all handlers require tightly coordinated shared state

nodes.name: Dependency Injection
nodes.summary: Provide required collaborators from a composition boundary instead of constructing them inside business behavior.
applicability: collaborator implementation or lifecycle varies independently
hidden construction prevents isolated testing or boundary control
tradeoffs: moves wiring complexity to a composition root
excessive injection can expose low cohesion or oversized services
avoid_when: the value is an immutable implementation detail with no boundary role
a service locator would replace explicit dependencies with runtime lookup

nodes.name: Repository
nodes.summary: Expose persistence operations in domain or use-case terms while containing storage queries and mapping at a boundary.
applicability: application behavior needs stable aggregate-oriented persistence operations
storage records or ORM mechanics leak into inward-facing code
tradeoffs: generic repositories can erase useful query semantics
mapping and transaction ownership must remain explicit
avoid_when: the repository only mirrors every ORM method
simple read models are clearer as focused queries

edges.rationale: Strategy localizes independently varying algorithms or policies behind one behavioral contract.
State localizes behavior and transitions that currently branch on explicit state.
Factory Method contains selection of one concrete product when creation varies.
Abstract Factory fits when several related products vary together as a family.
Builder can make staged assembly and completion-time validation explicit.
Adapter localizes translation between an external interface and the local contract.
Decorator composes independent optional behavior without subclass combinations.
Facade centralizes cohesive, repeated subsystem workflows behind a focused entry point.
Composite provides uniform operations when leaves and containers share valid semantics.
Observer decouples an event producer from a changing set of consumers.
Command gives an operation identity and lifecycle beyond an immediate method call.
Chain of Responsibility replaces a central ordered dispatcher with composable handlers.
Dependency Injection moves collaborator choice and lifecycle to a composition boundary.
Repository contains persistence details behind use-case-oriented operations.
Both move conditional behavior, but Strategy represents caller-selected policy while State represents behavior driven by lifecycle state.
Use Factory Method for one varying product and Abstract Factory for compatible product families.
A factory may select a builder when both creation policy and staged assembly vary.
A command can carry a request through a handler chain when both request lifecycle and routing vary.
A composition root may inject collaborators produced by explicit creation policy.
Adapter changes an interface to fit a local contract, while Facade simplifies a cohesive subsystem workflow.
